sections.section: Optional: Cuarto Real Alto (separate timed visit)

tracks.title: Welcome to the Real Alcázar
tracks.where: Outside the Puerta del León on the Plaza del Triunfo, the main visitor entrance: a battlemented wall with an arched gateway, and a tile panel of a lion above the arch. Stand clear of the entry line.
tracks.what: Real Alcázar de Sevilla, Puerta del León (Lion Gate), 14th-century gateway of Pedro I's time with a later tile lion; overview of the site and of how this guide works.
tracks.listen: What the Alcázar is, eleven centuries in one breath, and how the numbers, the three lengths and the Extras of this guide work.

tracks.title: 1 · Patio del León — The Lion Gate and a lost theatre
tracks.where: Just inside the Lion Gate, in the Patio del León: an open courtyard with four garden beds, between the entrance wall and the far wall, which is pierced by a triple arch leading on to the larger courtyard beyond.
tracks.what: Puerta del León and the León–Montería portal: gate, wall and tower casing of one building campaign under Pedro I, 1350s (radiocarbon centred on 1368); later tile lion (maker and date not established); site of the Corral de la Montería theatre, 1620s–1691; largely cleared 1936–37 to designs by Juan Talavera.
tracks.listen: Why the Lion Gate is Pedro's and not Almohad, how this courtyard was a theatre for sixty years, and why the triple arch is off-centre.

tracks.title: 1 · Patio del León — Eleven centuries on one site
tracks.where: Still in the Patio del León, the first courtyard inside the Lion Gate, with the triple arch leading on.
tracks.what: A timeline of the Alcázar: 913 (Abd al-Rahman III), the Abbadid palace al-Mubarak, the Almohad residence, 1248, Alfonso X's Gothic palace, Pedro I's palace, the Casa de la Contratación, the 1526 wedding, the 19th-century Bourbon rooms, the 1931 cession to the city, the royal residence today.
tracks.listen: Eleven centuries in two minutes, so you can tell whose wall is whose as you walk.

tracks.title: 2 · Sala de la Justicia — Alfonso XI's hall
tracks.where: Inside the Sala de la Justicia, off the far left-hand corner of the Patio del León as you face the triple arch: a small square hall with plaster-covered walls and a fountain set into the middle of the floor.
tracks.what: Sala de la Justicia, a square Mudéjar hall built at the time of Alfonso XI of Castile, 14th century (around the 1340s); plasterwork with plant motifs and heraldic shields; floor fountain.
tracks.listen: A king's victory, a Christian hall in Islamic dress, and the first step towards Pedro's palace.

tracks.title: 3 · Patio del Yeso — What the Almohads left
tracks.where: In the Patio del Yeso, reached only through the Sala de la Justicia: a small courtyard with a long pool, small garden beds beside it, and a portico of arches carrying a lattice of interlaced plaster arches.
tracks.what: Patio del Yeso, part of an Almohad residence of about 1190 (the Islamic "Palacio del Yeso"); sebka lattice; residence of Pedro I in 1358; rediscovered 1855; restored 1918–20 and 1969–71.
tracks.listen: The courtyard where Pedro lived before his palace was ready, and the Almohad lattice he lived under.

tracks.title: 4 · Patio de la Montería — Reading the courtyard
tracks.where: In the Patio de la Montería, just through the triple arch from the Patio del León: the Alcázar's largest open courtyard, dominated by the tall, richly decorated front of King Pedro's palace, which faces you across it. The Cuarto del Almirante runs along the right-hand side.
tracks.what: Patio de la Montería, the Alcázar's main courtyard; the façade of Pedro I's palace (begun from 1356); the Cuarto del Almirante, seat of the Casa de la Contratación 1503–1717; the porticoed gallery to the Patio del Crucero.
tracks.listen: Your bearings in the main courtyard: the palace front, the House of Trade, the way to the Gothic palace, and what the name means.

tracks.room: No. 5 · Fachada del Palacio del Rey Don Pedro
tracks.title: 5 · Fachada del Palacio del Rey Don Pedro — A king's name in two scripts
tracks.where: In the Patio de la Montería, close to the front of King Pedro's palace: the tall, richly carved façade with its central doorway, bands of lettering high on the front and blue-and-white tiles.
tracks.what: Façade of the palace of Pedro I, inscription dated Spanish era 1402 (= 1364); Gothic Castilian inscription framing the Nasrid motto "wa-la ghaliba illa Allah" in Kufic script on blue-and-white tiles; palace begun from 1356, finished by 1366.
tracks.listen: Why a Christian king of Castile signed his palace in Gothic letters around an Arabic motto from Granada, and why the Alhambra was not his model.

tracks.title: 6 · Cuarto del Almirante — The Casa de la Contratación
tracks.where: Inside the Cuarto del Almirante, the range behind a row of columns along the right-hand side of the Patio de la Montería as you face the palace front, signed as the Casa de la Contratación: the first rooms of the Admiral's Quarter, before the old audience hall with the painting of the Virgin.
tracks.what: Cuarto del Almirante (Cuarto de los Almirantes), seat of the Casa de la Contratación from its founding by Real Provisión of the Catholic Monarchs, Alcalá de Henares, 20 January 1503, until its move to Cádiz in 1717.
tracks.listen: How the trade and shipping of the Spanish Atlantic were run from these rooms for two centuries, including the slave trade.

tracks.room: No. 7 · Capilla de la Virgen de los Navegantes
tracks.title: 7 · Capilla de la Virgen de los Navegantes — Alejo Fernández
tracks.where: In the old audience hall of the Casa de la Contratación, at the end of the Cuarto del Almirante: stand in front of the altarpiece whose central panel shows the Virgin spreading her cloak over a crowd, with ships on the sea below.
tracks.what: Alejo Fernández (attributed), Virgen de los Navegantes or Virgen de los Mareantes, 1531–36, central panel of an altarpiece for the chapel of the Casa's audience hall; side panels St Sebastian, St James, St Elmo, St John on Patmos; owned by Patrimonio Nacional, kept in the Alcázar.
tracks.listen: Who tradition puts under the Virgin's cloak, why all those names are disputed, and the people in the background who have no name at all.

tracks.title: 10 · Patio de las Doncellas — The king hailed as sultan
tracks.where: At the near end of the Patio de las Doncellas, in the corner where the bent passage from the palace door brings you in: a large arcaded courtyard with a long central pool between sunken garden beds, its walls lined with tile and carved plaster.
tracks.what: Patio de las Doncellas, central courtyard of the palace of Pedro I (begun from 1356, finished by 1366); Arabic dado inscriptions naming Pedro "sultan"; the life and death of Pedro I (1334–1369) and his remains' journey to Seville Cathedral.
tracks.listen: How a Christian king came to be greeted as sultan on his own walls, how he lost his throne and his life, and the long road his body took back to Seville.

tracks.title: 10 · Patio de las Doncellas — The buried garden
tracks.where: At the edge of the long central pool in the Patio de las Doncellas: the pool runs down the middle of the courtyard between two sunken garden beds, below the level of the walkways and arcades.
tracks.what: The sunken garden of Pedro I's Patio de las Doncellas: walks, pool and beds found on 22 Aug 2002 under a 16th-century level (excavations 2002 and 2004, directed by M. Á. Tabales); pool gone by 1584, courtyard paved with a central fountain under Felipe II; garden restoration by the Patronato, 2004–05; 16th-century Renaissance columns.
tracks.listen: How a garden buried for four centuries came back to light, and why King Pedro may never have walked in it.

tracks.room: No. 13 · Salón del Techo de Carlos V
tracks.title: 13 · Extra · The chapel under the emperor's ceiling
tracks.where: Inside the Salón del Techo de Carlos V, through its door in the long side of the Patio de las Doncellas: a long hall under a dark Renaissance coffered ceiling, with carved busts among the coffers.
tracks.what: Salón del Techo de Carlos V, in the palace of Pedro I: the king's oratory, designed as a chapel; Renaissance coffered ceiling installed in the early 1540s (1542 Pleguezuelo; 1543 andalucia.com), with busts of human figures; a tiled altarpiece of 1504 by Niculoso Pisano, now lost except for fragments. Next door, no. 14, Sala de los Infantes.
tracks.listen: A royal chapel inside Pedro's palace, a lost tiled altarpiece, and a ceiling named after an emperor who was not there to see it.

tracks.title: 15 · Salón de los Embajadores — The dome of 1427
tracks.where: Inside number 15, the Salón de los Embajadores: a square hall under a gilded wooden dome, with tiled and carved walls, wrought-iron balconies high up and a painted frieze of royal portraits below the dome. Stand near the middle, clear of the doorways.
tracks.what: Salón de los Embajadores (Salón de la Media Naranja), main hall and throne room of Pedro I's palace, finished 1366 (Arabic door inscription, era 1404 / year 767); gilded wooden dome by Diego Ruiz, 1427, said to replace an earlier dome; wrought-iron balconies under Felipe II, late 16th century; frieze of portraits of the monarchs by Diego de Esquivel, 1599.
tracks.listen: Why the gold overhead is sixty years younger than the hall, and how the doors date the room in two calendars.

tracks.title: 15 · Salón de los Embajadores — The night the emperor married
tracks.where: Still in number 15, the Salón de los Embajadores, under the gilded dome. Stay where you stood for the last stop.
tracks.what: The marriage of Charles V (Charles I of Spain) and Isabel of Portugal, Seville, night of 10–11 March 1526: betrothal by words of present consent by Cardinal Salviati in the "media naranja"; nuptial Mass after midnight by the Archbishop of Toledo at an altar set up in a chamber of the palace (Sandoval; Pleguezuelo places it in no. 13); godparents the Duke of Calabria and the Countess of Haro.
tracks.listen: How an emperor married a cousin he had never met on the night he reached Seville, and how the marriage ended.

tracks.room: No. 16 · Salón del Techo de Felipe II
tracks.title: 16 · Extra · The Peacock Arch and two ceilings
tracks.where: In number 16, the Salón del Techo de Felipe II, beside the Salón de los Embajadores: a long room under a curved wooden ceiling. Number 17, the Sala de los Reyes Católicos, lies on the way to the Patio de las Muñecas.
tracks.what: Salón del Techo de Felipe II, named after its semi-barrel wooden ceiling; the Peacock Arch (Arco de los Pavones) leading to the Salón de los Embajadores; Sala de los Reyes Católicos, with a wooden ceiling of ribbons and heraldic emblems. No dates or makers sourced.
tracks.listen: Two rooms named after what is over your head, and an arch named after birds.

tracks.title: 18 · Patio de las Muñecas — Columns from older buildings
tracks.where: In number 18, the Patio de las Muñecas: a small courtyard, the smallest on the visit, with slender columns and carved plaster arches at ground level and galleries rising above. Stand near the arch closest to the way you came in.
tracks.what: Patio de las Muñecas, private courtyard of Pedro I's palace; reused Caliphal and Roman columns and capitals; small carved heads at the springing of the arch nearest the entrance hall; two upper floors of the 19th century; surrounding rooms remodelled under the Catholic Monarchs.
tracks.listen: The tiny faces that name the courtyard, columns older than the palace, and the woman legend puts here.

tracks.title: 18 · Extra · The Prince's rooms and a forgotten passage
tracks.where: Beside number 18, the Patio de las Muñecas, at the rooms known as the Cuarto del Príncipe, the Prince's rooms, where the restored passage to the gardens begins. Do not take the passage now.
tracks.what: Cuarto del Príncipe (not named in the leaflet legend); the historic passage from the Patio de las Muñecas to the Jardín del Príncipe, restored and reopened to the public in 2025, with its tiles, plasterwork and floors recovered. Prince Juan, son of the Catholic Monarchs, born in Seville in 1478, died 1497.
tracks.listen: A passage that lay unused for decades, and the prince who gave these rooms their name.

tracks.title: 31 · Patio del Crucero — Alfonso X's Gothic palace
tracks.where: In number 31, the Patio del Crucero, the courtyard of four garden beds beside the Gothic palace, reached from the corner of the Patio de la Montería. The Gothic palace runs along its right-hand side as you come in. Look for the stone Baroque portico that leads into the Gothic halls.
tracks.what: Patio del Crucero, largely of the Islamic period; the Gothic palace built by Alfonso X in the 13th century over the remains of the Almohad palace; its lower level survives as the "Baños de Doña María de Padilla" (no. 34); damaged in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, repaired (the Salón de los Tapices, no. 32, lost its vaults to late Baroque arches), with a stone Baroque portico added in the later 18th century.
tracks.listen: How a learned Castilian king built a Gothic palace over an Islamic one, and the three ages you can read in one courtyard.

tracks.room: No. 32 · Salón de los Tapices y Capilla
tracks.title: 32 · Salón de los Tapices — The conquest of Tunis
tracks.where: In number 32, the Salón de los Tapices: a long, high hall in the Gothic palace, its walls hung with very large tapestries of a sea campaign. The chapel opens off this hall.
tracks.what: Tapestries of Charles V's conquest of Tunis, 1535: 18th-century replicas woven in Madrid by the Vandergoten family's royal manufactory for Felipe V, after the twelve-panel set designed by Jan Cornelisz Vermeyen and Pieter Coecke van Aelst and woven by Willem de Pannemaker in Brussels, 1548–1554 (gold, silver, silk and wool). Originals (ten survive) and the replica set belong to Patrimonio Nacional. Number of panels on view: count on site (O15).
tracks.listen: Why these famous tapestries are copies, who drew the campaign as it happened, and how they frame the sack of Tunis.

tracks.room: No. 32 · Salón de los Tapices y Capilla
tracks.title: 32 · Extra · The chapel of the Gothic palace
tracks.where: In the chapel of the Gothic palace, which belongs to number 32, the Salón de los Tapices y Capilla: a small room under ribbed Gothic vaults, with a tiled dado and an altarpiece holding a painted Virgin.
tracks.what: Capilla del Palacio Gótico: medieval rib vaults; Renaissance tiled dado, 16th century; altarpiece with a copy of the Virgen de la Antigua (Seville Cathedral), attributed to Diego de Castillejo; Domingo Martínez, La Virgen de los Reyes entre San Hermenegildo y San Fernando, 1742; La Inmaculada con donante y Cristo como sacerdote. What is on view: O16.
tracks.listen: A copy of one of Seville's oldest paintings, under vaults from Alfonso X's palace.

tracks.title: 33 · Sala de las Bóvedas — The vaulted hall
tracks.where: In number 33, the Sala de las Bóvedas, also called the Salón Gótico, the hall on the garden side of the Salón de los Tapices: a long hall under Gothic vaults, its walls tiled to about two metres with figures and plants, with a glass-panelled gallery looking into the garden.
tracks.what: Sala de las Bóvedas (Salón Gótico, Sala de Fiestas) of Alfonso X's Gothic palace; Mannerist tile dado of the 16th century to about 2 m, figures and plants, many on a yellow ground; two naval tapestries made for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition.
tracks.listen: The hall of celebrations, its tiles, and two tapestries far younger than they look.

tracks.room: No. 34 · Baños de Doña María de Padilla
tracks.title: 34 · Baños de Doña María de Padilla — A garden underground
tracks.where: Inside number 34, the Baños de Doña María de Padilla, entered from the garden through the palace wall at the head of the Jardín de la Danza: a long, dim pool under Gothic vaults, below the Patio del Crucero. Stand where you can see along the length of the water.
tracks.what: Lower level of the Patio del Crucero: a sunken summer garden, its vaults made Gothic under Alfonso X (13th century), remodelled under Felipe III with a Mannerist fountain (remains at one end of the pool) and an opening to the Jardín de la Danza. Named after María de Padilla by legend only. Game of Thrones: Ellaria Sand's arrest.
tracks.listen: Why this is neither a bath nor a cistern, and why the name is a love story that never happened here.

tracks.title: 35 · Jardín del Príncipe — The poet king
tracks.where: In number 35, the Jardín del Príncipe, the garden of four beds round a small fountain below the palace, entered through a colonnade. Number 36, the Columna de Al-Mutamid, is marked in the narrow garden you came through beside the palace. The garden end of the restored passage from the Patio de las Muñecas is here.
tracks.what: Jardín del Príncipe; Columna de Al-Mutamid (no. 36; describe only as seen, O19); al-Mu'tamid (1040–1095), third and last Abbadid king of Seville, poet; his court at the palace of al-Mubarak, "the Blessed"; exile to Aghmat; the gardens' Islamic origins and Renaissance redesign under Charles I and Felipe II; more than 20,000 plants of at least 187 species.
tracks.listen: The poet king of Seville, the wife he freed, and the exile he never came back from.

tracks.title: 38 · Jardín de la Danza — Water from Carmona
tracks.where: In number 38, the Jardín de la Danza, one of the small Italianate gardens below the palace, near the steps up to the Mercury pool. Two columns stand on its upper level, by the steps.
tracks.what: Jardín de la Danza, one of the Italianate gardens "de las Damas, la Danza, Troya, Galera y Flores"; dated by the Alcázar's exhibition text to the 18th century, with a small stage for dances and performances; two columns on the upper level by the steps to the Mercury garden, damaged by falling branches in Storm Bernard (2023) and restored in 2024; the garden water system fed by the Carmona aqueduct; Felipe III's opening from the Baths.
tracks.listen: How water reached these gardens, and the two columns that a storm knocked about.

tracks.title: 39 · Estanque de Mercurio — Mercury and his twin
tracks.where: At the edge of number 39, the Estanque de Mercurio: the big raised pool with a gilded bronze Mercury standing on a sphere in the middle, a long painted gallery wall along its far side, opposite the way up from the Danza.
tracks.what: Mercury group, designed by Diego de Pesquera and cast in bronze by Bartolomé Morel, added in 1576; the figure in the pool today is a gilded bronze replica made during the 2022–2024 restoration. Pool of Islamic origin, redesigned in the 16th century, fed by the Carmona aqueduct.
tracks.listen: Why the god in the pool is a faithful twin of the 1576 bronze, and the gold that the cleaners found on the original.

tracks.title: 40 · Galería del Grutesco — An old wall in costume
tracks.where: Beside number 40, the Galería del Grutesco: the long painted gallery wall that runs along the far side of the Mercury pool, opposite the way up from the Jardín de la Danza.
tracks.what: Galería del Grutesco, Vermondo Resta's transformation of an Islamic wall, 1613–1621; paintings by Diego de Esquivel, finished in 1629 after seven years; paintings restored from July 2023.
tracks.listen: How a plain wall of the Islamic Alcázar was dressed up as a Renaissance grotto, and what the painters put on it.

tracks.title: 41 · Extra · The water organ
tracks.where: Beside number 41, the Fuente de la Fama: the fountain in a semicircular niche set into the same long wall as the Grutesco, beyond the end of the Mercury pool.
tracks.what: Fuente de la Fama, a 17th-century organ fountain with a hydraulic chamber, restored in 2006 by Leonardo Lombardi with Rodney Briscoe.
tracks.listen: The only 17th-century organ fountain preserved in Spain, and the two men who made it work again.

tracks.title: 44 · Pabellón de Carlos V — A pavilion for a wedding
tracks.where: In front of number 44, the Pabellón de Carlos V: a small, square, tiled pavilion standing in an open space at the far end of the formal gardens.
tracks.what: Pabellón (Cenador) de Carlos V, by Juan Hernández, built in honour of the 1526 marriage of Charles V and Isabel of Portugal, on the origin of a Muslim qubba; 16th-century tiles from the Polido brothers' workshop; floor tracing the old labyrinth; integral restoration reported in 2026.
tracks.listen: A pavilion built to honour an emperor's wedding, which the emperor himself never saw.

tracks.title: 44 · Extra · Dorne: the Alcázar on screen
tracks.where: Still beside number 44, the Pabellón de Carlos V, the small tiled pavilion where the Dorne fight scene was filmed.
tracks.what: Game of Thrones, season 5, filmed at the Real Alcázar from October 2014, aired 2015: the Alcázar as the Water Gardens of Dorne. Also Lawrence of Arabia.
tracks.listen: Which scenes of Dorne were filmed where in the Alcázar, set straight from the Film Commission's own list.

tracks.title: 45 · Cenador del León — The lion's pavilion
tracks.where: By the pool in front of number 45, the Cenador del León, at the end of the open space beyond the Pabellón de Carlos V: a garden pavilion standing just behind a pool presided over by a lion.
tracks.what: Cenador del León, built 1644–1645 to designs by Diego Martín Orejuela, painted decoration by Juan de Medina, tiles supplied by Benito Valladares; its pool older, with a 14th-century phase and a 16th-century enlargement, rebuilt after the pavilion; archaeological watch during the 2017 restoration found late-medieval heraldic plaster, very probably of Pedro I's time (a working hypothesis), on the east and north walls of the pool's walkway, not on the single-phase pavilion.
tracks.listen: A seventeenth-century pavilion named after the lion in its pool, and the medieval heraldry archaeologists found in the walls round its pool.

tracks.title: 46 · Extra · The twentieth-century gardens
tracks.where: In number 46, the Jardín Inglés, the garden of winding paths just beyond the Cenador del León; look for the sign with its name.
tracks.what: Jardín Inglés (46) and Jardín Marqués de la Vega Inclán (50), early 20th-century gardens in the English and French styles; the Puerta de Marchena bought by the Marquis de la Vega-Inclán on behalf of Alfonso XIII for the new gardens.
tracks.listen: How a royal garden kept growing into the twentieth century, in English and French fashions, and why a Gothic gateway came with it.

tracks.title: 51 · Puerta de Marchena — A gateway that travelled
tracks.where: In front of number 51, the Puerta de Marchena: a carved Gothic stone gateway standing in the garden, with wild-man figures holding shields.
tracks.what: Puerta de Marchena, former front of the Dukes of Arcos's palace in Marchena, built 1492 and reformed 1540; sculptures by Esteban Jamete, datable to 1544; design possibly linked to Juan Guas; bought by the Marquis de la Vega-Inclán on behalf of Alfonso XIII for the Alcázar's new gardens.
tracks.listen: How the front door of a ducal palace in another town ended up standing in a royal garden.

tracks.title: 53 · Apeadero — The way out
tracks.where: Inside number 53, the Apeadero, or just beyond it: the columned hall at the end of the visit that leads out into the Patio de Banderas.
tracks.what: Apeadero, by Vermondo Resta, 1607; from the 17th century the Alcázar's main access, today the visitors' exit. Patio de Banderas: within the oldest walled enclosure; Roman building of 60–30 BC found about 5 m down in the 2009–2013 excavations.
tracks.listen: Leaving through the Alcázar's old front door, over the oldest ground of all, with a last look back at the layers.

tracks.section: Optional: Cuarto Real Alto (separate timed visit)
tracks.room: No. 20 · Dormitorio de Isabel la Católica
tracks.title: CRA 20 · Extra · Isabel's rooms and a tiled altar
tracks.where: For the foot of number 19, the stair to the Cuarto Real Alto, before going up or after coming down; upstairs only where listening is allowed. It covers number 20, the Dormitorio de Isabel la Católica, and number 21, her chapel.
tracks.what: Cuarto Real Alto, the upper floor of King Pedro's palace (map rooms 20–30); in the queen's oratory, number 21, a tiled altar signed by Niculoso Francisco Pisano and dated 1504: the Visitation framed by the Tree of Jesse.
tracks.listen: The upper rooms of Pedro's palace, still a royal residence, and the signed tile altar made for Isabel the Catholic in the last year of her life.

tracks.section: Optional: Cuarto Real Alto (separate timed visit)
tracks.title: CRA 23 · Extra · A royal house still in use
tracks.where: For the Cuarto Real Alto visit, at number 23, the Comedor de Gala, the state dining room, or at the foot of the stair afterwards if listening upstairs is not allowed. It also covers number 22, the Antecomedor, and number 24, the Sala de Fumar.
tracks.what: Cuarto Real Alto rooms 22 Antecomedor, 23 Comedor de Gala and 24 Sala de Fumar; 19th-century Bourbon additions and refurbishments with tapestries, crystal lamps from La Granja, clocks, furniture and paintings; the upper floor as the head of state's official residence in Andalucía.
tracks.listen: Why these upper rooms look nineteenth-century, and how they still serve the King today.
